slides.title: Assessment. Hands-on practice of laboratory testing methods (final)
bullets: Hands-on practice of laboratory testing methods
Assessment — 6 h

slides.title: Lesson outline
bullets: Textbook material: Final review: pre-analytics and quality control; Final review: safety, equipment and basic methods

Practice: Q&A: 6 + 3

slides.title: Final review: pre-analytics and quality control
bullets: Quality control has three phases: pre-analytical (correct collection, transport, registration and storage of material), analytical and final (post-analytical); internal control is done daily, in every analytical series.
Internal control rests on regular testing of a standardised control material and recording results on a control chart.
Sources of analytical error: general laboratory factors, reagents, control material, samples and the instrument (calibration, cuvettes, optics).

slides.title: Final review: pre-analytics and quality control
bullets: Sample collection: minimal venous stasis, a suitable anticoagulant-to-blood ratio, no oxalate/EDTA for calcium, prevention of haemolysis; plasma is recommended for many enzymes.
Blood is recommended to be drawn in the morning, fasting, lying or sitting; diet, body position, drugs and physical activity affect the result.
In the final phase the result is checked against the referral and the same patient’s previous results, and the dispatch time is shown.

slides.title: Final review: safety, equipment and basic methods
bullets: All samples are potentially infectious: gloves, no mouth pipetting, single-use scarifiers, no glassware with chipped edges, hepatitis B vaccination.

slides.title: Final review: safety, equipment and basic methods
bullets: Acid or alkali exposure — rinse with plenty of water without neutralising; a cut with infected material — wash with soap under running water and disinfect with 70% alcohol or iodine.

slides.title: Final review: safety, equipment and basic methods
bullets: Clean and check the microscope before use; after immersion wipe the 100× objective with a soft cloth (no alcohol); balance tubes in the centrifuge and do not open the lid while it runs.

slides.title: Final review: safety, equipment and basic methods
bullets: In photometry optical density is proportional to colour intensity; most methods are measured in a 1 cm cuvette; when programming an instrument one enters the method name, reaction type, unit, temperature, calibration, volumes, filter, normal range and linearity limit.

slides.title: Final review: safety, equipment and basic methods
bullets: Physico-chemical methods: centrifugation, electrophoresis, chromatography, colorimetry, photometry and spectrophotometry.

slides.title: Final review: safety, equipment and basic methods
bullets: In the acid–base state blood pH is 7.35–7.45; buffer systems (haemoglobin, bicarbonate, protein, phosphate), the lungs and the kidneys keep it stable; BE is normally ±2.5 mmol/L.

slides.title: Types of systematic errors:
The following intralaboratory factors can affect test results:
options: Pipetting factor, principle of the method used

slides.title: Control material prepared from horse serum can be used in the following cases:
options: turbidity less than 0.2 units. Extinction (cuvette 0.3 cm; wavelength 630–690 nm)

slides.title: Not used in quality control of coagulation tests:
options: Fresh pooled plasma from many donors (at least 20 people), standard lyophilized human plasma for calibration
plasma prepared from human plasma with a precise concentration of coagulation factors (normal and pathological)
control plasma deficient in some coagulation factors
Fresh plasma obtained from a donor

slides.title: Quality management method that does not require control materials:
options: Study of parallel samples, repeat testing of the sample

slides.title: Interlaboratory quality control makes it possible to:
options: Compare the quality of work of several laboratories
Assess the quality of the methods used

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of hematological tests. Preparation of blood and bone marrow preparations for hematological examination?
bullets: 1. The preanalytical stage – more than half of laboratory errors occur at this stage: correct test ordering, patient preparation and identification, specimen collection, labeling, transport, receipt.

2. For CBC, venous blood in an EDTA tube (purple cap); follow the WHO-recommended order of draw (after citrate, before fluoride), fill the tube completely for the blood:anticoagulant ratio and immediately invert gently the number of times indicated by the tube manufacturer (to avoid clots and microclots).

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of hematological tests. Preparation of blood and bone marrow preparations for hematological examination?
bullets: 3. Capillary blood: the finger is well warmed, the first drop is removed, no squeezing (admixture of tissue fluid distorts the result).

4. Storage and transport: the specimen at room temperature, analyze as soon as possible; with prolonged storage MCV, platelets and the differential change; clotted, hemolyzed or incorrectly labeled specimens are rejected.

5. Smear preparation: a thin smear with a "tail" on a clean degreased slide; rapid drying, fixation (methanol) and staining by Romanowsky; prepare the smear from EDTA blood without delay (morphological artifacts).

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of hematological tests. Preparation of blood and bone marrow preparations for hematological examination?
bullets: 6. Bone marrow aspirate: several smears immediately from the aspirate (with particles), the rest in EDTA for flow cytometry/cytogenetics; a separate smear for Perls staining.

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of clinical biochemical tests. Collection, storage and preparation of biomaterial for testing in clinical biochemistry?
bullets: 1. Patient preparation: for many tests – in the morning, after 8–12 hours of fasting (glucose, TG, iron); avoid physical exertion, alcohol, smoking, stress; information about medications; diurnal variation (cortisol, iron).

2. Specimen collection: correct identification, short tourniquet time (a prolonged tourniquet raises protein, Ca, K), avoid fist clenching (K rises), WHO order of draw (EDTA contamination raises K and lowers Ca).

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of clinical biochemical tests. Collection, storage and preparation of biomaterial for testing in clinical biochemistry?
bullets: 3. Tubes: serum (with gel separator), heparinized plasma (fast result), fluoride/oxalate (glucose), EDTA (HbA1c), citrate (coagulation) – depending on the test.
4. Handling: centrifuge after clotting, separate serum from cells as soon as possible – glycolysis (glucose falls by ~5–7% per hour), release of K and phosphate; protect bilirubin from light.

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of clinical biochemical tests. Collection, storage and preparation of biomaterial for testing in clinical biochemistry?
bullets: 5. Storage: if analysis is delayed, serum at 2–8 °C or frozen (stability is test-specific); assess hemolysis, lipemia and icterus indices and account for interference.
6. Criteria for specimen acceptance and rejection: wrong tube, insufficient volume, hemolysis, unlabeled specimen – recorded (quality indicators).

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of hemostasis tests. Collection, storage and preparation of biomaterial for hemostasis testing?
bullets: 1. Anticoagulant: 3.2% (105–109 mmol/L) sodium citrate, blood:citrate ratio 9:1; the tube must be filled to at least ~90% of nominal volume – underfilling alters PT, aPTT, fibrinogen (aPTT is especially sensitive).
2. If hematocrit is >55%, correct the citrate volume (the plasma fraction is small – relatively too much citrate).

3. Collection technique: atraumatic venipuncture, short tourniquet time; with a butterfly set, because of the air space, a "discard" tube first; avoid heparin/EDTA contamination (order of draw – citrate tube before EDTA and heparin).

slides.title: Preanalytical stage of hemostasis tests. Collection, storage and preparation of biomaterial for hemostasis testing?
bullets: 4. Mixing: gently, according to the manufacturer's instructions (without shaking); clot, hemolysis, foam – reason for rejection.

5. Processing: centrifuge to obtain platelet-poor plasma; store and transport the specimen at room temperature (in the cold, factor VII may be activated and VIII/vWF lost), perform the test within the specified time; freeze for special tests.
6. Patient information: anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs), antiplatelet agents – stated on the requisition for interpreting the result.
